title: The clay lamp
hook: a thief took his iron lamp, so he bought a clay one, and the thief lost more (Discourses 1.18)

segments.voice: Yesterday: blind, not wicked, the wrongdoer who misjudged what's good, and your line, pity them instead. Did you manage pity instead of anger, even once? Day four hundred two.

Someone takes the package off your porch. Someone swipes your bike, your lunch from the office fridge, your parking spot. It's small, but it stings for days. You replay it. You check the doorbell camera. You tell five people. Epictetus had something stolen too, and his reaction is one of the most famous little stories in the Discourses. It involves a noise at the window, an empty spot by the shrine, and a trip to buy a cheaper replacement. Today: lychnos.
screen: `THE PACKAGE OFF YOUR PORCH.` → `IT STINGS FOR DAYS.` → `A NOISE AT THE WINDOW.`

segments.voice: Still in Discourses book one, chapter eighteen, right after yesterday's teaching about blindness. Epictetus tells his students: I kept an iron lamp beside the little shrine of my household gods. I heard a noise at the window, ran down, and found the lamp gone. And then, he says, I thought it over. The thief wanted a lamp; that's understandable. So tomorrow, I told myself, you'll find a clay one. A person only loses what they have. Notice the arithmetic. An iron lamp was a decent possession. A clay lamp costs very little, and gives the same light. Epictetus lost almost nothing that mattered. The thief, as Epictetus sees it elsewhere in the Discourses, paid a much higher price: for a lamp, he became a thief. He gave up his own honesty, his trustworthiness, which no one could have taken from him, in exchange for a piece of iron. Who lost more? Epictetus also explains why we get so angry at thieves: because we admire the things they take. If you didn't prize your clothes so much, he says, you wouldn't rage at the one who steals them. And there's a funny ending to the story, from outside the Discourses. The writer Lucian, a generation later, mocks a man who paid three thousand drachmas for Epictetus' clay lamp after the philosopher died, as if owning it would make him wise. The cheap lamp became an expensive treasure, which is exactly the kind of admiring Epictetus warned about.
screen: `THE IRON LAMP, STOLEN.` · `TOMORROW, A CLAY ONE.` · `FOR A LAMP, HE BECAME A THIEF.` · `THE CLAY LAMP SOLD FOR A FORTUNE.` · then, large: `A CLAY LAMP.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Think of one small thing that was taken from you, recently or long ago: an object, some money, credit for your work, a seat. Notice how tightly you're still holding it. Now picture the clay lamp: a simple, cheap thing that gives the same light. What would your clay lamp be here? Let yourself buy it, in your mind. Then notice what you still have that no one could take. The bell holds the time.
Lychnos. Greek for the lamp Epictetus lost: an iron one, replaced for a little with a cheap clay lychnos, while the thief gave up his own honesty.
Your line: a clay lamp. If something small is taken from you today, let it go and buy the clay lamp: replace it simply, and keep what can't be stolen. Day four hundred two.

howItsDone: Many readers keep Epictetus' clay lamp as a shorthand for letting small losses go: replacing what's gone simply and refusing to give up their own calm or character over it.

fork.setup: you're Epictetus. you run downstairs at a noise and find your iron lamp stolen. what do you do?
options: report it and bar the windows.
tell yourself: tomorrow you'll find a clay one.
fork.reveal: he decided to buy a cheap clay lamp, reasoning that a person only loses what they have.

original.note: Greek lychnos: an oil lamp, the kind Epictetus kept by his household shrine.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't let people walk all over you.
what it means: a small loss costs you a little iron; the thief gives up his honesty, so he loses more.
what a scholar hears: Lucian's satire 'The Ignorant Book-Collector' reports the clay lamp sold for 3,000 drachmas, an ironic coda to a story about not prizing things.

notes: Discourses 1.18 paraphrased: the iron lamp by the household gods, the noise at the window, 'tomorrow you'll find an earthen one', 'a man loses only what he has', and 'don't admire your clothes and you won't be angry with the thief'. Confirm.
'For a lamp he became a thief' is attributed in the script to 'elsewhere in the Discourses' (I believe 1.29); confirm the chapter.
Lucian, Adversus Indoctum 13: Epictetus' earthenware lamp bought for 3,000 drachmas. Confirm section number and amount.
The 'clay lamp' carry reads as 'a clay lamp'; title word 'The clay lamp' kept exactly.

Reviewer edit: the text does not say the theft happened at night; 'noise in the night' and 'empty shelf' changed to 'noise at the window' and 'empty spot by the shrine'. Lucian wrote some decades after Epictetus died (c. 135); 'a generation later' is approximate.
